source.title: Channel Normalization in Convolutional Neural Network avoids Vanishing Gradients

record.tranche_reason: Compares channel normalization with no normalization and reports effects on optimization in convolutional networks, using a single training example rather than the claim version’s stated benchmark settings.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own comparisons of normalized and unnormalized networks. Figure-only outcomes are recorded as such. The 100-image ImageNet replication is described without numerical results; cited work is not treated as this study’s result.
record.test_reason: The study compares training convergence with and without channel normalization in single-example convolutional networks. Channel normalization is equivalent to batch normalization at batch size one, so the convergence comparisons test V6 in a new setting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors report that channel normalization prevents vanishing gradients and enables efficient single-example convolutional fitting. They prove exponentially slow convergence without normalization for a restricted linear CNN and analyze how normalization changes gradients; they do not prove a matching fast-convergence guarantee with normalization.
record.recipe_differences: Compares channel normalization with no normalization in single-example convolutional networks; uses gradient descent, but not the benchmark architectures, datasets or accuracy-speed measures specified in V6.
record.method_sensitivity: Normalization condition (learned channel-normalization parameters, fixed scale/shift, or none); network setting (multi-channel nonlinear CNN versus single-channel linear CNN); initialization and step-size assumptions in the theoretical analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: Without normalization, a Gaussian-initialized single-channel linear CNN requires exponentially many gradient-descent steps in depth under the theorem's assumptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Certain deep linear convolutional networks have exponentially slow gradient-descent convergence under the specified initialization and signal assumptions.

fits_no_version.finding: Channel normalization produces smaller tails in initialization gradient-norm distributions for linear and nonlinear convolutional networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Channel normalization changes initialization gradient distributions and reduces extreme gradient norms in these tested networks.

record.problems: The main empirical examples are narrow, mostly single-example fitting or small toy CNNs. Several outcomes are qualitative and figure-based, with no numerical error or uncertainty estimates. The claimed 100-image ImageNet replication is described without numerical results.
record.rows_left_out: The text says the Figure 1 effect was reproduced on 100 randomly chosen ImageNet images and related generators including upsampling networks, but gives no separate quantitative values or distinct result beyond the stated qualitative effect, so no additional row is recorded. Figure 3 loss-landscape plots are illustrative rather than a separately reported training outcome.

untested.parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, label corruption, and model-size effects.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious local minima, and additional student neurons.
Depth comparisons in plain versus residual networks, identity shortcuts, and shortcut-free training recipes.
Comparative learning speed and trainable depth under activation-matched, Gaussian, or orthogonal initializations.
Learning rates relative to initial stability thresholds, catapult recovery, and edge-of-stability dynamics.
Classification accuracy gains, higher learning-rate tolerance, the named benchmark architectures and datasets, and Fixup residual networks.

missing.what: A separate fixed-scale-and-shift normalization condition for the single-channel linear CNN: it reaches a good minimum and performs similarly to learned normalization.

record.verdict_notes: The narrow setting and untested benchmark comparisons do not justify limits_scope. Gradient-distribution measurements provide mechanistic evidence but cannot independently establish training-speed or learning-rate-tolerance effects.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training classification error, random or corrupted labels, model size, and the stated SGD/Adam benchmark recipes.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and varying student width.
Depth versus training error in plain and residual networks; identity shortcuts; the cited special initialization and Fixup results are prior work.
Comparisons of activation-matched, Gaussian, or orthogonal initialization and trainable depth.
Training above the stability limit, curvature or sharpness dynamics, and divergence as a function of learning rate.

Batch normalization comparisons on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet; accuracy-speed comparisons; learning-rate tolerance; and Fixup residual networks. This study tests channel normalization in convolutional generators and toy convolutional networks.
